implementation_notes: The standard library defines the classical operations on every Sequence and Collection: map, filter, compactMap (map and drop nil), flatMap, reduce, plus contains/allSatisfy/first(where:) as short-circuiting terminals. They are eager and return an Array - the stdlib source for Sequence.map reserves a ContiguousArray and returns it - so the chain replaces a for-in loop with an accumulator while keeping every intermediate value available. lazy and AsyncSequence are the lazy and asynchronous counterparts, and reduce(into:) is the terminal for accumulating into a buffer.
code_sketch:
let emails = people
    .filter { $0.isActive }
    .map(\.email)
    .sorted()
    .prefix(10)                    // still a slice of the eager array

let total = orders.reduce(into: 0) { $0 += $1.amount }   // terminal
pitfalls: map/filter allocate a new Array per stage and evaluate eagerly, even when a later stage would drop most elements.
prefix/dropFirst results are views into the base collection: keeping the slice alive keeps the whole array alive, and Array(...) is needed to snapshot it.
String building inside reduce is quadratic unless reduce(into:) (or joined()) is used, because every concatenation copies.

variants.name: Lazy sequences (.lazy)
variants.implementation_notes: .lazy gives the sequence operations explicit permission to be lazy: the LazySequenceProtocol documentation states that operations taking closures 'are normally eager: they use the closure immediately and return a new array', while 'when you use the lazy property, you give the standard library explicit permission to store the closure and the sequence in the result, and defer computation until it is needed'. The chain becomes a LazyMapSequence/LazyFilterSequence composition with no intermediate arrays, which is the recommended form for large collections, long chains, early termination and unbounded sequences. Laziness applies only while the static type is known to conform to LazySequenceProtocol, so the lazy step must come first.
variants.code_sketch:
let firstBig = numbers.lazy
    .map { $0 * $0 }
    .filter { $0 > 100 }          // no intermediate arrays
    .prefix(3)                    // stops after 3 survivors

for value in firstBig { print(value) }   // pulls on demand
pitfalls: Laziness lasts only while the static type conforms to LazySequenceProtocol: passing the result to a function taking [Element] silently evaluates the whole chain.
Using map/forEach only for side effects drops or defers them; use a for-in loop instead.

variants.name: AsyncSequence pipelines
variants.idiom_name: AsyncSequence.map / filter / reduce over for await
variants.implementation_notes: For elements that arrive asynchronously (a URL stream, a file handle, an actor-decoded feed) the same operators exist on AsyncSequence: Apple's documentation describes AsyncSequence as resembling Sequence but adding asynchronicity, with map and filter returning AsyncMapSequence/AsyncFilterSequence that 'don't eagerly await the next member of the sequence', and reduce as a terminal. It replaces a collection pipeline whenever the stages are async or the source is I/O; consumer code iterates with for await (or for try await), and the task's cancellation is what stops an infinite source.
pitfalls: An AsyncSequence is lazy and single-use: without a for await/terminal nothing is read, and iterating it twice re-runs the asynchronous source.
Errors travel through the sequence type (AsyncThrowingMapSequence), and nothing stops an infinite source except task cancellation - a forgotten cancellation keeps the work running.
